explanations.explanation: That's the charge. Jehu, the seer who confronts the king, asks him, “Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD?” (2 Chronicles 19:2). It's a question, and a pointed one. Jehu says it straight to the king's face, which takes some nerve.

Nothing about the treasury comes up, friend. Jehu never says a word about money or the temple. His charge is about who Jehoshaphat helped: “Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD?” (2 Chronicles 19:2). Nobody's counting silver in this scene.

The text says the opposite of running. Jehoshaphat "had returned safely to his home in Jerusalem" (2 Chronicles 19:1), and Jehu meets him there. What Jehu calls out is helping the wicked and loving those who hate the LORD (2 Chronicles 19:2). The king's feet were never the problem.

Wrath is the word. Jehu says, “Because of this, the wrath of the LORD is upon you” (2 Chronicles 19:2). Those are heavy words to get when you've just walked in your front door. Hold on, though, because Jehu isn't done talking.

Blessing would be a much nicer welcome home, friend, but that's not what Jehu says. His words are, “Because of this, the wrath of the LORD is upon you” (2 Chronicles 19:2). The "because of this" points back to helping the wicked and loving those who hate the LORD.
Peace sounds lovely, and I wish it fit here. Jehu says, “Because of this, the wrath of the LORD is upon you” (2 Chronicles 19:2). It's a hard message, and the king hears it right at his own home.
True! Right after the hard word, Jehu says, “However, some good is found in you…” (2 Chronicles 19:3). That "however" matters. Jehu names the correction and the good in the same breath.

It's the other way around, friend. Jehu says, “However, some good is found in you…” (2 Chronicles 19:3). The hard word comes first, and then he says what's good in the king. I'd take that kind of honesty any day, even if my ears would be burning.

Yes! Jehu says, “…you have removed the Asherah poles from the land and have set your heart on seeking God.” (2 Chronicles 19:3). Jehoshaphat took those poles out of the land himself. Jehu says it right alongside the hard word, so both are on the table.
No temple walls here, friend. Jehu names two things: the king “removed the Asherah poles from the land” and has “set your heart on seeking God.” (2 Chronicles 19:3). Neither one involves a trowel.

explanations.answer: He fed the hungry in Judah
explanations.explanation: Feeding the hungry is a good thing to do, but it isn't what Jehu points to. He says the king “removed the Asherah poles from the land” and “set your heart on seeking God.” (2 Chronicles 19:3). That's the good Jehu finds in him.

explanations.answer: He turns the people back to God
explanations.explanation: That's it. The text says he "turned them back to the LORD, the God of their fathers" (2 Chronicles 19:4). It's a long walk, too, from Beersheba to the hill country of Ephraim. And he went out "once again," so this wasn't his first trip.

No armies get gathered here. The text says Jehoshaphat went out among the people and "turned them back to the LORD, the God of their fathers" (2 Chronicles 19:4). The war was already behind him. This trip is about the people's hearts.

explanations.answer: He collects taxes for the palace
explanations.explanation: No tax collecting in this verse, friend. Jehoshaphat goes out among the people and "turned them back to the LORD, the God of their fathers" (2 Chronicles 19:4). The text doesn't mention the palace at all.

The LORD, yes. Jehoshaphat tells the judges, “…you are not judging for man, but for the LORD, who is with you when you render judgment.” (2 Chronicles 19:6). That changes how heavy every ruling feels. It also means they're never judging alone.

The king is the one giving the speech, friend, but he doesn't point the judges back to himself. He says, “…you are not judging for man, but for the LORD, who is with you when you render judgment.” (2 Chronicles 19:6). So the answer is the LORD.

The people are the ones standing in front of them, so I understand the guess. But Jehoshaphat says, “…you are not judging for man, but for the LORD, who is with you when you render judgment.” (2 Chronicles 19:6). The one they answer to is the LORD.

explanations.answer: With the LORD there is no partiality or bribery
explanations.explanation: That's the reason he gives. Jehoshaphat says, “Be careful what you do, for with the LORD our God there is no injustice or partiality or bribery.” (2 Chronicles 19:7). The judges are judging for the LORD, so their judging should look like His. Nobody gets special treatment in that courtroom.

explanations.answer: The LORD will remove any judge who turns aside
explanations.explanation: Jehoshaphat never says that. He tells them to be careful, “for with the LORD our God there is no injustice or partiality or bribery.” (2 Chronicles 19:7). His reason is about what the LORD is like. He doesn't threaten to remove anyone.

explanations.answer: The LORD keeps a record of every judgment
explanations.explanation: A record isn't mentioned here, friend. The reason he gives is, “…for with the LORD our God there is no injustice or partiality or bribery.” (2 Chronicles 19:7). Careful judges, because a fair LORD is behind them.

True! In Jerusalem, Jehoshaphat appointed “some of the Levites, priests, and heads of the Israelite families to judge on behalf of the LORD and to settle disputes.” (2 Chronicles 19:8). So the priests are right there in the mix. It's a mixed team, and nobody sits alone on that bench.

The text says otherwise, friend. Jehoshaphat appointed “some of the Levites, priests, and heads of the Israelite families to judge on behalf of the LORD and to settle disputes.” (2 Chronicles 19:8). Priests are named right in the middle of that list.

Not quite, friend. Jehoshaphat names bloodshed outright. Every dispute that comes before them counts, “whether it regards bloodshed or some other violation of law, commandments, statutes, or ordinances” (2 Chronicles 19:10). The small cases and the serious ones both land on that bench.

Right, it's False. Jehoshaphat says every dispute counts, “whether it regards bloodshed or some other violation of law, commandments, statutes, or ordinances” (2 Chronicles 19:10). Bloodshed is on the list by name. It's a heavy one, and the judges are told to take it seriously.

Guilt is the word. The judges are to warn them “so that they will not incur guilt before the LORD…” (2 Chronicles 19:10). Jehoshaphat adds that wrath won't come on the judges and their brothers either. Warning people early is part of the job.

Debt would be a different kind of trouble, friend, and the text doesn't go there. The judges warn people “so that they will not incur guilt before the LORD…” (2 Chronicles 19:10). The weight is before the LORD, not in a ledger.

Shame is close in feeling, but it isn't the word in the verse. The judges are told to warn them “so that they will not incur guilt before the LORD…” (2 Chronicles 19:10). Guilt before the LORD is what the warning is meant to prevent.

Yes, Amariah. Jehoshaphat says, “Note that Amariah, the chief priest, will be over you in all that pertains to the LORD…” (2 Chronicles 19:11). Matters of the LORD go to the chief priest. The king's matters go to someone else, and we'll get to him.

Zebadiah, the ruler of the house of Judah, does have a job, but it's a different one. The verse says he's over “all that pertains to the king.” (2 Chronicles 19:11). Matters of the LORD belong to Amariah, the chief priest. Those two jobs are split on purpose.

The text splits the jobs, friend. Amariah, the chief priest, is “over you in all that pertains to the LORD,” and Zebadiah son of Ishmael is over “all that pertains to the king.” (2 Chronicles 19:11). Each man gets his own lane. No sharing, and no traffic jams.
